verses.translation_literal: A song of the ascents, of Solomon. If YHWH does not build a house, [in] vanity have its builders toiled in it; if YHWH does not guard a city, [in] vanity has the guard kept awake.
verses.translation_dramatic: A song for the pilgrim climb, set in Solomon's name. Unless the LORD himself raises the house, the hands that raise it labor for nothing; every stone they set is set in vain. Unless the LORD keeps the city, the watchman may stand awake through the long dark, his eyes burning, and keep his vigil for nothing.
verses.directors_commentary:
Open on a building site and a city wall at night, the two places where ancient people felt safest because they had worked hardest. The singer picks the two great human projects, shelter and security, and says both rest on someone other than the workers. The Hebrew is built on a matched pair of verbs, 'build' (banah) and 'guard' (shamar), each answered by a pair of words for futile effort: shav' ('vanity, emptiness') and then the verbs 'toiled' ('amalu) and 'kept awake' (shaqad). Play the repeated 'in vain' as a drumbeat, not as a scold.

The heading 'of Solomon' (lishlomoh) is ambiguous. The lamed can mean 'by' or 'for' or 'concerning'; Ibn Ezra and Radak take it as 'on account of Solomon', the song of David's hopes for the son who would build the Temple. The 'house' can then be the Temple, or an ordinary house, or a dynasty ('house of David'), and an actor should not pick just one. The KJV's 'Except the LORD build the house' is archaic ('except' for 'if... not') and adds two articles the Hebrew lacks: it says 'a house' and 'a city', any house and any city. The KJV also writes 'the watchman waketh', which hides that shaqad is a strong verb, 'to keep wakeful, to stay on the alert', and its noun cousin comes from the almond tree (shaqed), the first tree to wake in spring. The 'ascents' (hama'alot) is the title of fifteen psalms (120-134), songs for climbing to Jerusalem for the pilgrim festivals, so a crowd is singing this on a road, with the city in view.

philological_notes.note: 'The ascents', the title shared by Psalms 120-134. It is usually taken as songs sung while going up to Jerusalem, or on the steps of the Temple; the tradition of fifteen steps is later rabbinic. The root is 'to go up'.

'Emptiness, nothing, vanity'. It is the same word as in the third commandment ('do not lift up the name of YHWH in vain'). Here it opens the second half of each line, so the futility is placed right after the 'if not' clause, the hinge of the whole verse.

'To keep awake, be vigilant'. Radak takes it as 'to busy oneself eagerly', and Meiri and Metzudat Zion as 'to hasten, persist', so the watchman's wakefulness is not the sleepless fear of a man in danger but the work of a professional.

verses.translation_literal: [In] vain [it is] for you, [you who] rise early, [you who] delay sitting, [you who] eat the bread of the toils; so he gives to his beloved sleep.
verses.translation_dramatic: Empty, all of it, for you who drag yourselves up before the light, who put off the hour of sitting down until the night is old, who chew the bread of aching labor. Yet he gives to the one he loves, and gives it freely: sleep.
verses.directors_commentary:
The speaker turns from the builders and watchmen to the audience itself: 'for you'. Play the first half as a man shaking his head at a tired crowd, the second as a quiet smile. The three participles ('rising early', 'delaying sitting', 'eating') are a picture of a whole working day, from before sunrise to after dark, with meals taken on the run. 'The bread of the toils' ('lechem ha'atzavim') calls back the curse on Adam in Genesis 3:17-19, where the ground yields food only 'in toil' ('itzavon') and 'by the sweat of your face' you eat bread. The singer is telling his audience that the labor of the curse does not buy security.

The last line is the hard one. 'So he gives to his beloved sleep' can be read as 'in the same way, he gives sleep' (shena' is the object, the gift), or as 'he gives to his beloved while he sleeps', so that the gift arrives without effort, and Radak reads it that way, the Temple and kingship granted to Solomon without his labor. The KJV 'for so he giveth his beloved sleep' keeps the first reading and its 'for' is not in the Hebrew, which has only ken ('so, thus'); the BBE's 'in sleep' takes the second. The word for 'beloved' (yadid) is the name Yedidyah, 'beloved of YHWH', that Nathan gave Solomon (2 Samuel 12:25), which explains why the heading names Solomon. Shena' is spelled with a final alef here instead of the usual he, a rare spelling that Radak and Metzudat Zion both remark on. This is not a sermon against hard work: Meiri notes that no sage ever praised idleness, only trust placed in effort alone.

philological_notes.note: 'Those who rise early', from the root that gives shekhem, the 'shoulder', as in 'to load the beast early in the morning'. Ibn Ezra reads it as going early to the marketplace, Radak as Absalom's early rising to seduce the people at the gate.

'The toils, the pains', the plural of 'etzev, from the same root as 'itzavon, the toil of Genesis 3:17. The KJV's 'sorrows' makes it a feeling; the Hebrew names the strain of work, so 'bread of toil' is closer.
'Sleep', with an unusual final alef in place of the normal he (shena). Radak and Metzudat Zion both note the spelling.

verses.translation_literal: Behold, an inheritance of YHWH [is] sons; a reward [is] the fruit of the belly.
verses.translation_dramatic: Look, then, and see what no labor could have bought. Sons: they are the LORD's own inheritance, handed over into your keeping. The fruit of the womb: it is wages, a payment set in your hand by him.
verses.directors_commentary:
Play the turn from verse 2 plainly: the one who rose before light and ate the bread of aching labor is told that the household he is straining to secure is not a thing his toil can produce. Sons are given. In a village economy a family without sons had no one to work the field, defend the gate, bury the father or carry on his name and his land, so this is a statement about survival and status as much as tenderness. 'Inheritance' (nachalah) is land-language: a plot passed down within a clan and held ultimately of YHWH, who is Israel's true owner. Here the picture reverses, and the sons are what YHWH hands down to the man.

The KJV's 'heritage' is a fair, if archaic, rendering of nachalah, and 'the fruit of the womb' is accurate: beten means both belly and womb. The literal layer keeps 'belly' because the Hebrew word is the plain bodily one, and the line is earthy: birth is as physical as a harvest. The Hebrew is also verbless and has no 'his', where the KJV adds 'is his reward', which smooths the clause into a tidy sentence. Say it as two blunt statements, with a beat between them. 'Reward' (sakhar) is wages, what is paid for work done. The commentators (Ibn Ezra, Metzudat David, Malbim) hear this as YHWH paying for deeds. The psalm's point is that the wage comes from him and not from the builder's sleepless toil: the same word, set against the 'labor' of verse 2, makes the irony.

philological_notes.note: A hereditary holding, usually land passed down in a family. Calling sons YHWH's nachalah gives them the weight of a family estate that is not bought but handed on. Radak reads it as the good YHWH gives his friend in this world; Meiri reads 'of YHWH' as a superlative, the finest inheritance.

Wages or reward, a payment for work done. Ibn Ezra glosses it as the reward of the deed, and Malbim reads it as given to those who stand well before YHWH. The psalm sets it against the fruitless toil of verse 2: a payment that human labor alone cannot secure.

Belly, and by extension womb. The literal layer keeps 'belly'; 'womb' as in the KJV and STEPBible is also correct. Rashi, with a different idea, takes the belly as the heart where Torah is kept (Prov 22:18).

verses.translation_literal: Like arrows in the hand of a warrior, so [are] the sons of the youth.
verses.translation_dramatic: As arrows lie in a warrior's hand, sharp and ready and aimed at the future, so are the sons born in a man's youth.
verses.directors_commentary:
The image shifts from the field to the battlefield. An arrow is useless in itself; it matters only in the hand of someone strong enough to draw and aim it. The comparison cuts two ways. A father is the warrior and the sons are his reach, the means by which his name and his claim go out to places he cannot walk. But the singer also hints that sons need a hand to launch them. The Hebrew word is gibbor, the 'mighty man', the title of David's elite fighters, so the figure is a seasoned soldier, not a boy with a bow.

'Sons of the youth' (benei hane'urim) are children born while the father is young. The word ne'urim, 'youth', is a plural of abstraction, like 'old age' (zeqenim). Ibn Ezra adds 'and not the sons of old age', since a man who fathers early lives to see them grown and strong while he is still strong himself. The KJV 'children of the youth' misses the 'sons' again, and its 'mighty man' is fine but flat, since gibbor suggests a champion. The arrow was a precious thing: a hardened shaft with a flint or bronze tip, cut and fletched by hand.

philological_notes.note: 'Warrior, mighty man', from the root of 'to be strong'. It is the title of David's elite soldiers (the 'mighty men'), so the image is of a champion, not of any archer.
'The youth', an abstract plural. Ibn Ezra reads it as 'and not the sons of old age'; Rashi, taking the sons as disciples, reads 'those a man raises up from his youth'.

verses.translation_literal: How blessed [is] the man who has filled his quiver with them; they will not be ashamed when they speak with enemies in the gate.
verses.translation_dramatic: Blessed, blessed is the man whose quiver is full of them. When they stand in the gate and face the men who hate him, they will not be shamed, and they will not be silenced.
verses.directors_commentary:
The last verse gives the payoff: a man with a full quiver. The Hebrew 'ashrei is not the KJV's 'happy'; it is an exclamation, 'oh, the blessedness of', a congratulation from outside, which the Psalter uses to open Psalm 1. The quiver ('ashpah) is the household itself, as Radak and Meiri say. Count the arrows: more sons means more voices.

The finale is not on a battlefield but at the city gate. The gate was the courthouse, the town hall and the marketplace of an ancient town, where the elders sat to judge disputes, witness contracts and settle land claims (as in Ruth 4). To 'speak with enemies in the gate' is to face an accuser or an opposing litigant, and a man alone, with no clan behind him, could be shamed, overruled or robbed. A man with many grown sons arrives with a bench of supporters. The KJV 'but they shall speak' adds an adversative the Hebrew does not have: it is 'for' (ki), 'because' or 'when', and the verb is plural, so the sons are the speakers, and it is not clear whether 'ashamed' applies to the father too. 'Enemies' is the plain word, 'oyevim, and the KJV keeps it. Rashi's reading, in which the 'enemies' are scholars who contradict one another over the law, is a later reinterpretation, not the surface sense.

philological_notes.note: 'Oh the blessedness of', a plural construct used as an exclamation. It describes a state of flourishing seen from outside and is not a command or a wish.
'His quiver'. Rashi glosses it as the case for arrows and gives a medieval French word for it; Metzudat Zion cites Jeremiah 5:16, 'their quiver is an open grave'.
'In the gate', the open space inside the city gate where elders sat for judgment and public business. Metzudat Zion cites Zechariah 8:16, 'judge truth and peace in your gates'.
